\chapter{Synthesis --- Claiming, and Not Claiming}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-subjuntivo}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose the mood by deciding whether I am willing to assert the thing at all.}

Indicative: this is so. Subjunctive: I am not saying this is so.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — claiming, and not claiming}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-sintesis-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Say \emph{hablas}, then \emph{hables}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the second one is actually doing}]
Those two forms are not two tenses. They are two \textbf{stances}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Hablas español.} — I am telling you this is so. \textbf{Quiero que hables español.} — I am not telling you anything is so.
\end{quote}

In the first, you put a fact on the table and stood behind it. In the second, nothing has been claimed at all: the speaking has not happened, and might not. The mood is the difference, and the difference is about \textbf{what you are willing to assert}.

That is the whole of it, and it is worth holding onto, because every remaining use of this mood — and there are many — is a version of the same move. Wishing, doubting, denying, hoping: none of them puts a fact on the table.

\begin{quote}
Indicative: \emph{this is so.} Subjunctive: \emph{I am not saying this is so.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— ¿\textbf{Hablas} español? — Ana quiere que \textbf{hable} español. — \textbf{Ojalá hables} mucho.
\end{quote}

Three lines, three stances. The first asks about a fact. The second reports somebody's wish, so nothing is asserted. The third wishes it outright.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Ojalá} deserves a last look, because it explains itself.

It is Arabic — \emph{wa-šā' allāh}, \textquotedblleft{}and may God will it\textquotedblright{} — carried into Spanish over eight centuries of al-Andalus and kept long after the religion behind it stopped being the speaker's. A Spanish speaker saying \emph{ojalá} today is uttering a prayer in a language they do not speak, to a God the sentence no longer names.

And it can only ever take this mood. Of course it can: a thing God has yet to will is, by definition, not a fact you can assert.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three-line exchange, and name the stance of each line
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until choosing the mood feels like choosing what you mean.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the indicative do that the subjunctive does not? (\textbf{Claim that something is so.}) Why can \emph{ojalá} never take the indicative? (Because a thing not yet willed is not a fact.) And what language is \emph{ojalá}? (\textbf{Arabic} — a prayer that outlived the religion behind it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
